_meta.model: claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 (MODELS.FAST), 1 route / two states (log, review patterns)
_meta.why_v2: Ground-up rebuild (commit 622372be) replaced the six-mode weekly-audit design (Daily Check-In, Planner, Recharge, Weekly Audit, Say Yes?, Journal — capacity/budget arithmetic, cost-per-hour math, weekly_budget/recovery_time sections) with two states: log one interaction, review patterns across logs. The v1 cases below (main-audit, week-planner, quick-check, recharge-minimal) tested endpoints (/plan, /quick-check, /recharge) and fields (energy_score, drains, rechargers, weekly_budget) that no longer exist and were replaced wholesale. This re-record was overdue — golden went unrecorded at v2's own rebuild and was failing 0/4 by the time this correction pass found it.
_meta.why_v2_1: Owner review of live output found the pattern-reasoning engine overclaiming beyond the data in five ways: (1) converting a contrast between two logs into an implied cause ('something about the pace or dynamic differed') instead of naming every candidate feature and saying the log doesn't establish which mattered; (2) statistical-sounding language ('does not predict') from a 3-entry sample; (3) test_next experiments that changed more than one variable at once (or, once fixed, asked the visitor to wait for a deliberately MISMATCHED combination of two conditions to break a confound — still a compound ask); (4) energy-transfer language ('cost'/'added'/'reduced') for what is only a before/after self-rating, not a battery measurement; (5) calling a 2-4-observation split a 'pattern' before the evidence actually earned that word. CONTRACT gained a CONTRAST DISCIPLINE section, a rewritten PATTERN THRESHOLD with an explicit evidence-count ladder and a banned-word list, and an ACTION section requiring single-variable experiments with a mandatory fallback when the candidate variables are confounded. Frontend: the 'My patterns (N)' tab was renamed 'What I'm noticing (N)' across all 13 languages.
_meta.why_v2_2: A second owner review, after living with the corrected output, found four remaining implementation issues: (1) the raw internal on-ness enum (not_much/a_lot) was leaking into generated prose instead of the plain-English form the input form already showed — fixed at the CODE level (a new onnessLabel() helper humanizes the value before it ever reaches the model's prompt, so the token literally cannot be echoed, not just a prompt instruction hoping the model complies); (2) a contrast invented an unstated duration ('duration: not specified vs. implied longer') — added an explicit NEVER INFER duration rule and stripped 'duration' from the CONTRAST DISCIPLINE default feature list unless both entries actually supplied one; (3) the single-variable experiment language still overstated what casual observational logging can establish ('will help separate on-ness from group size', 'independent of group size') — ordinary logs cannot hold other variables constant, so ACTION was rewritten to ban 'separate'/'isolate'/'independent' as claims and require purely observational framing ('see whether a repeated relationship appears'); (4) summary language occasionally treated 'energy' as a measured quantity ('ended with you 2 points higher in energy') rather than keeping the language attached to the rating — added an explicit rule and example. While re-verifying, live testing also surfaced a stochastic third-person voice leak ('The visitor rated their energy...') that the corrections had not touched — CONTRACT had never had an explicit VOICE section (unlike the same-session SpiralStopper fix), so one was added with a wrong/right example. Frontend: added two more rotation examples (3→5, matching the session's five-example convention) and removed the 'Refresh patterns' button — saveLog() now clears stale results automatically, so the only action after saving is 'Log another interaction'; revisiting the patterns tab after a new log shows the same single 'look for patterns' action used on first visit, not a distinct refresh concept.
_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run cases (npm run check:golden sea). Diff for QUALITY not exact match: HTTP 200, no truncation. GUARDS: validateResult() in backend/routes/social-battery-advisor.js keys on summary.headline/body being present; caps worth_noticing<=3, contrasts<=2, not_enough_to_tell<=4; forces test_next to one well-shaped object; summary.counts is always recomputed in code from the actual submitted logs, never trusted from the model. Every correction above is prompt-enforced (CONTRACT) except the enum humanization, which is code-enforced in the logText builder (onnessLabel()) — when eyeballing new captures, grep the JSON for 'not_much'/'a_lot' (should never appear), 'predict', 'pattern' (below 5 comparable observations), 'cost'/'drained'/'restored'/'added energy', 'isolate'/'separate'/'independent' used as a CLAIM (not as a hedge denying capability, which is fine), 'implied' + a duration word, and 'the visitor' (should always be 'you'/'your'). DO NOT reverse: the array caps, the recomputed counts, the onnessLabel() code fix, or any CONTRACT discipline above.

logs.note: Six people. I knew everyone, but the conversation moved fast.
Small group and I mostly listened.
We talked for about half an hour.

summary.headline: Three interactions produced three different outcomes: one ended lower, one unchanged, and one ended higher.
summary.body: The dinner with friends ended 2 points lower despite knowing everyone present. The team meeting ended unchanged. The phone call with your sister ended 2 points higher, and you reported feeling not much on during it.

worth_noticing.title: The interaction where you felt not much on was the only one that ended higher.
worth_noticing.evidence: Phone call with your sister: energy 2→4, on-ness not much. The dinner (a lot on) ended lower. The team meeting (some on) ended unchanged.
worth_noticing.meaning: Worth continuing to track: whether interactions where you feel less on tend to end with higher ratings than interactions where you feel a lot on. With only one log in each direction, this is too early to treat as a pattern, but it is a contrast worth watching.

contrasts.title: Dinner ended lower; phone call ended higher
contrasts.first: Dinner with friends: 4→2, on-ness a lot, six people, conversation moved fast
contrasts.second: Phone call with sister: 2→4, on-ness not much, about half an hour
contrasts.question: On-ness differed (a lot vs. not much), group size differed (six vs. two), and setting differed (dinner vs. phone call). This log does not establish which of these, if any, mattered to the different outcomes.

test_next.observation: The phone call with lower on-ness ended higher; the dinner with higher on-ness ended lower. Worth testing whether on-ness itself tends to accompany different before-and-after outcomes.
test_next.experiment: Keep logging as usual. Pay attention to your on-ness rating across your next several ordinary interactions, and notice whether higher on-ness, lower on-ness, or both appear alongside different kinds of before-and-after outcomes.
test_next.watch_for: Whether a repeated relationship appears between how much you felt you had to be on and whether your before-and-after rating ended higher, lower, or unchanged.

not_enough_to_tell: Whether group size, the pace or dynamic of conversation, familiarity with people, or any other feature of these interactions affected the outcomes — too many things differed between the dinner and phone call to point to one.
How the team meeting's unchanged rating relates to your other two experiences — only one entry in that category.

logs.note: About 25 relatives, lots of small talk.
Big crowded room, many new people.

summary.headline: Large gatherings where you felt a lot on ended lower; small interactions where you felt not much on ended higher.
summary.body: Three interactions with 20+ people and a lot of on-ness ended 2-3 points lower. Two interactions one-on-one with not much on-ness ended 2 points higher. The split is clean across these five logs.

worth_noticing.title: Large groups with a lot of on-ness ended lower; one-on-one interactions with not much on-ness ended higher
worth_noticing.evidence: Work happy hour (20+ people, a lot on): 4→2. Family reunion (25 people, a lot on): 4→1. Conference mixer (big crowded room, many new people, a lot on): 3→1. Coffee with close friend (just two, not much on): 3→5. Walk with neighbor (quiet, just the two, not much on): 2→4.
worth_noticing.meaning: These two kinds of interaction produced opposite outcomes in every example so far. You have only two examples on the higher end, so continue watching whether one-on-one interactions with lower on-ness consistently end higher, or whether something else about those particular interactions mattered. You also have only three examples on the lower end, though they are consistent.

contrasts.title: Work happy hour vs. coffee with close friend: opposite outcomes despite both being social
contrasts.first: Work happy hour (20+ people, a lot on): ended 2 points lower
contrasts.second: Coffee with close friend (just two, not much on): ended 2 points higher
contrasts.question: Group size and on-ness both differed between these interactions. This log does not establish which of those two, if any, mattered — or whether something else about the particular people, setting, or the nature of the interaction itself made the difference.

test_next.observation: The contrast between large-group-with-a-lot-on and one-on-one-with-not-much-on showing opposite outcomes.
test_next.experiment: Keep logging as usual. Pay attention to how much you feel you have to be 'on' in your next several interactions, and notice whether higher on-ness repeatedly appears alongside lower before-and-after ratings, and lower on-ness repeatedly appears alongside higher ratings.
test_next.watch_for: Whether on-ness and your before-and-after outcome repeatedly appear together in a consistent direction, or whether they did not line up the same way across different interactions.

not_enough_to_tell: Whether group size alone accounts for the difference, or whether on-ness is what mattered, or whether they mattered together.
Whether the specific people (close friend vs. new people vs. coworkers) shaped the outcome.
Whether the same outcome would happen if you were in a large group but felt not much on, or in a one-on-one but felt a lot on.

logs.note: I feel like I am heading toward a bigger crash, not just tired from this one call.

summary.headline: One log: back-to-back client calls left you 2 points lower, with a note that this feels like heading toward something larger.
summary.body: You rated your energy 3 before and 1 after, while feeling a lot on. Your own note flags concern about a bigger crash ahead, not just fatigue from this single session.

worth_noticing.title: Your note about heading toward a bigger crash
worth_noticing.evidence: You logged one interaction (back-to-back client calls, a lot on, energy 3→1) and added a note that this feels like heading toward a bigger crash, not just tired from this one call.
worth_noticing.meaning: This suggests you may be tracking something beyond what a single log can show — a sense of accumulation or direction over time. One log is not enough to establish whether you are approaching an overload, but your own observation is real and worth taking seriously. This belongs in Before the Crash, which can help you track what a full-scale crash looks like for you and what the warning signs are.

not_enough_to_tell: Whether back-to-back calls (versus single calls or other interaction types) consistently leave you lower.
Whether a lot of on-ness consistently goes with lower energy outcomes, or whether the outcome varies.
Whether you are actually approaching a crash, or what that would look like for you specifically.

handoff.reason: Your note explicitly says you feel like you are heading toward a bigger crash. Before the Crash can help you identify what a crash looks like for you and what the earliest warning signs are.
